exercises.prompt: How many IPv4 addresses are in the block `198.51.100.0/22`?

feedback.message: Not yet — /22 is the length of the fixed prefix in bits, not a count of addresses.
Not yet — with a 22-bit prefix, 32 − 22 = 10 bits are free, giving $2^{10}$ addresses.
Not yet — that is $2^{22}$. The prefix is fixed; the *remaining* 10 bits vary.

hints: An IPv4 address has 32 bits; the first 22 are fixed by the prefix.
exercises.solution: A /22 fixes the first 22 bits and leaves $32 - 22 = 10$ bits free, so the block has $2^{10} = $ **1024** addresses: `198.51.100.0` to `198.51.103.255`. In Python, `ipaddress.ip_network("198.51.100.0/22").num_addresses` gives 1024. Each bit shorter doubles the block: a /24 has 256 addresses, a /16 has 65,536.

exercises.prompt:
A router's forwarding table contains:

| prefix | next hop |
| --- | --- |
| `0.0.0.0/0` | ISP |
| `10.0.0.0/8` | core |
| `10.42.0.0/16` | campus |
| `10.42.7.0/24` | library |

Where does it send a packet for `10.42.9.3`?

options.label: library
options.feedback: Not yet — `10.42.7.0/24` covers only `10.42.7.0` to `10.42.7.255`. The third byte here is 9.

options.label: core
options.feedback: Not yet — `10.0.0.0/8` does match, but a longer, more specific prefix matches too, and the most specific match wins.

options.label: ISP
options.feedback: Not yet — the default route is used only when nothing more specific matches.

hints: List the prefixes that contain the address, then pick the longest.
exercises.solution: **campus**. The address matches `/0` (everything), `/8` (first byte 10) and `/16` (first two bytes 10.42), but not the `/24`, which requires the third byte to be 7. Longest-prefix match chooses the most specific route, `/16`. This rule lets a network announce a large block while carving out special cases inside it, such as the library's subnet, without listing every address.

exercises.prompt: For which of these applications is UDP (or a protocol built on UDP) a natural choice? Select all that apply.

options.label: A live video call
options.feedback: Yes: a frame that arrives late is useless, so retransmitting it (as TCP would, while holding up everything behind it) only adds delay. Calls tolerate a little loss better than delay.

options.label: A DNS lookup
options.feedback: Yes: a query and its answer usually fit in one datagram each, and the client simply retries if no answer comes.

options.label: Downloading a software update that must arrive byte-for-byte intact
options.feedback: Not yet — every byte matters and order matters, which is exactly what TCP's reliable byte stream provides. (HTTP/3 also does this over QUIC, which builds TCP-like reliability on UDP; plain UDP alone would not.)

options.label: A fast-paced online game's position updates
options.feedback: Yes: only the latest position matters; an old update that was lost should be skipped, not resent.

options.label: An SSH session to a remote server
options.feedback: Not yet — every keystroke and every byte of output must arrive, in order. SSH runs over TCP.

hints: Ask: is a late piece of data still useful? And does the application need every byte in order?
exercises.solution: **(a)**, **(b)** and **(d)**. UDP fits when data is time-sensitive (late is as bad as lost), when exchanges are single small messages that can be retried, or when the application wants to implement its own reliability, as QUIC does. TCP fits when every byte must arrive in order, as for files, web pages (before HTTP/3), email and remote shells.

exercises.prompt: A user's round-trip time to a web server is 80 ms, and to their DNS resolver also 80 ms. Nothing is cached. Loading the page needs one DNS round trip (the resolver already knows the answer), a TCP handshake, a TLS 1.3 handshake and one HTTP request/response. Ignoring processing time and bandwidth, how many milliseconds pass before the first byte of the HTML arrives?

feedback.message: Not yet — count again: DNS, TCP, TLS 1.3 and the HTTP request each take one round trip.
Close — that would be right with TLS 1.2, whose full handshake takes two round trips. TLS 1.3 needs only one.
Not yet — that counts only two round trips. Each of DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP needs its own.

hints: Count round trips: DNS, TCP handshake, TLS 1.3 handshake, HTTP request.
Multiply the number of round trips by 80 ms.
exercises.solution: DNS (1 RTT) + TCP handshake (1) + TLS 1.3 handshake (1) + HTTP request and response (1) = 4 round trips, so $4 \times 80 = $ **320 ms** before the first byte. With HTTP/3 over QUIC the transport and TLS handshakes are combined into one round trip, giving 240 ms; with a cached DNS answer and an already open connection, a later request needs only 80 ms. That is why latency, not bandwidth, usually dominates page-load time.

exercises.prompt: A browser has a cached copy of `/logo.png` with `ETag: "v7"`. It sends `GET /logo.png` with the header `If-None-Match: "v7"`, and the logo has not changed. Which response should the server send?

options.label: `304 Not Modified`, with no body
options.feedback: Yes: the cached copy is still valid, so the server saves bandwidth by not sending the image again.

options.label: `200 OK`, with the image
options.feedback: Not quite — that works, but it wastes the whole point of the conditional request: the client already has these bytes.

options.label: `404 Not Found`
options.feedback: Not yet — the resource exists; 404 would make the browser think the logo is gone.

options.label: `301 Moved Permanently`
options.feedback: Not yet — the logo has not moved. 301 tells the client to use a different URL from now on.

hints: The client is asking: "send it only if it is no longer version v7".
exercises.solution: **`304 Not Modified`**. `If-None-Match` makes the request conditional: the server compares the client's ETag with the current one, and if they match it replies 304 with headers but no body, telling the client to use its cached copy. This revalidation is a large part of how the web avoids resending unchanged images, scripts and stylesheets. RFC 9110 defines these semantics for every version of HTTP.

exercises.prompt:
Write `parse_response(raw)`, which takes a complete HTTP/1.1 response as `bytes` and returns a tuple `(status, headers, body)`: `status` is the status code as an `int`; `headers` is a `dict` whose keys are header names in **lower case** and whose values have surrounding spaces removed; `body` is the `bytes` after the blank line, cut to `Content-Length` bytes if that header is present. Lines end with `
`, and the header section ends with an empty line (`

`). Header values may themselves contain colons.
exercises.tests:
raw = (b"HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found\r\n" b"Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8\r\n" b"content-length: 9\r\n" b"X-Request-Id: abc:123 \r\n" b"\r\n" b"not here!extra bytes of the next response") status, headers, body = parse_response(raw) assert status == 404 and isinstance(status, int) assert headers["content-type"] == "text/plain; charset=utf-8" assert headers["content-length"] == "9" assert headers["x-request-id"] == "abc:123", "split each header line at the first colon only" assert body == b"not here!" status, headers, body = parse_response(b"HTTP/1.1 204 No Content\r\nServer: demo\r\n\r\n") assert (status, headers, body) == (204, {"server": "demo"}, b"") status, headers, body = parse_response(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\n\r\n

Sannu!

") assert status == 200 and body == b"

Sannu!

", "without Content-Length, the body is everything after the blank line" print("All tests passed!")
hints: `raw.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")` splits the head from the body at the first blank line.
Decode the head (HTTP headers are ASCII; `"iso-8859-1"` is a safe choice) and split it into lines on `"\r\n"`. The first line is the status line, like `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found`.
For each header line, `name, _, value = line.partition(":")` splits at the first colon only. Store `name.strip().lower()` and `value.strip()`.
exercises.solution:
```python
def parse_response(raw):
    head, _, body = raw.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")
    status_line, *lines = head.decode("iso-8859-1").split("\r\n")
    status = int(status_line.split(" ", 2)[1])
    headers = {}
    for line in lines:
        name, _, value = line.partition(":")
        headers[name.strip().lower()] = value.strip()
    if "content-length" in headers:
        body = body[:int(headers["content-length"])]
    return status, headers, body
```

The status line has three parts separated by spaces, but the reason phrase may contain spaces itself (`Not Found`), so split at most twice. Header names are case-insensitive by the standard, so normalising them to lower case lets code look them up reliably. `partition(":")` splits at the *first* colon, keeping values such as `abc:123` or URLs intact. `Content-Length` matters because one connection can carry many responses one after another: it tells the parser where this body ends and the next response begins. A production parser must also handle chunked transfer encoding, repeated headers, and hostile input.

exercises.prompt: Implement the **Internet checksum** of RFC 1071, used in IPv4, TCP and UDP headers. `internet_checksum(data)` treats `data` (bytes) as a sequence of 16-bit **big-endian** words (padding an odd-length input with a zero byte at the end), adds them up, repeatedly folds any carry above 16 bits back into the low 16 bits, and returns the bitwise complement of the result as an integer from 0 to 65535. Do not use the `struct` module.
exercises.tests:
hdr = bytes.fromhex("45 00 00 3c 1c 46 40 00 40 06 00 00 c0 00 02 0a c6 33 64 07")
assert internet_checksum(hdr) == 0x3231, hex(internet_checksum(hdr))
filled = hdr[:10] + bytes([0x32, 0x31]) + hdr[12:]
assert internet_checksum(filled) == 0, "a header with its checksum filled in sums to zero"
assert internet_checksum(b"") == 0xFFFF
assert internet_checksum(b"\x00\x01\xf2\x03\xf4\xf5\xf6\xf7") == 0x220D, "the example from RFC 1071"
assert internet_checksum(b"\xab") == internet_checksum(b"\xab\x00"), "pad odd lengths with a zero byte"
assert internet_checksum(b"\xff\xff" * 1000) == 0
print("All tests passed!")
hints: Each word is `(data[i] << 8) | data[i + 1]` for even `i` (big-endian: the first byte is the high byte).
